prompt:
# Lesson Reconciliation Prompt

## Mission

Support the two internal Lesson Reconciliation tasks for exactly one Lesson:

- `lesson_candidate_clustering`: group candidate IDs only.
- `lesson_cluster_evaluation`: evaluate one validated cluster or a small batch
  of validated clusters into clean lesson-local teachable concepts.
- `lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`: repair a deterministic Phase 4b
  quality failure for targeted candidates only.

The input candidates come from Self-study Extraction and Metadata-only
Extraction. There is no top-down lesson extraction in this pipeline branch.

## Quick Start

First inspect `task`.

If `task` is `lesson_candidate_clustering`, return clusters only. Every
`input_candidate_ids` item must appear exactly once across cluster `candidate_ids`.
Do not create accepted concepts, pruning decisions, evidence, or provenance.

If `task` is `lesson_cluster_evaluation`, read the provided `clusters`,
`candidates`, and `input_candidate_ids`. Create the smallest clean set of
lesson-local concepts for those clusters only. Return accepted concepts plus one
`candidate_assignments` row for every input ID in the batch.

If `task` is `lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`, read the quality audit,
current reconciled candidates, and target candidates. Decide whether each target
candidate should be represented by a new accepted concept, merged into an
existing accepted concept, or pruned. Do not return `review`.

## Concept Standard

A lesson-local concept is one teachable idea small enough for the Companion to
check with one to three focused questions. It is not a source title, activity,
workbook label, technology name, vague topic, name-drop, incidental mention, or
tiny fragment that belongs inside a stronger concept.

Source-backed does not automatically mean lesson-worthy. A candidate can be
grounded in a source and still be incidental, off-lesson, too broad,
administrative, setup-oriented, or better represented inside another concept.
Accept only candidates that fit the Lesson's title, description, related labels,
and candidate evidence as teachable content for this Lesson.

## Clustering Workflow

1. Group duplicates and near-duplicates that likely describe the same teachable
   idea in this Lesson.
2. Keep distinct prerequisite, implementation, evaluation, or application ideas
   in separate clusters.
3. Prefer small coherent clusters over broad topic buckets.
4. Put operational setup, installation, licensing, career, administrative, and
   generic programming candidates in their own clusters unless the Lesson
   metadata clearly makes them central content.
5. Do not prune during clustering unless an input is clearly unrelated to the
   Lesson; if uncertain, put it in its own cluster for evaluation.
6. Every input candidate ID must appear exactly once across all clusters. Never
   emit empty clusters or invented candidate IDs.

## Evaluation Workflow

1. Treat Source Body candidates as the strongest evidence.
2. Merge duplicates and near-duplicates across Self-studies when they teach the
   same idea inside the provided cluster batch.
3. Split compound or messy candidates into cleaner accepted concepts when one
   input candidate supports multiple teachable ideas.
4. Accept Metadata-only candidates only when Workbook Metadata fills a real
   lesson gap not already covered by Source Body candidates.
5. Prefer lesson coherence over source-by-source preservation, but never drop a
   source-backed candidate silently.
6. Preserve useful granularity. Do not merge distinct definitions, pipeline
   steps, limitations, implementation methods, evaluation methods, or
   applications merely because they share a broad topic.
7. Reject off-lesson or low-transfer material even when it is source-backed:
   setup commands, environment configuration, licensing/legal administration,
   certification/career advice, repository mechanics, dataset download
   utilities, and routine file I/O should be accepted only when the Lesson
   metadata clearly makes that material central teachable content.
8. Use `used_in` when a candidate directly supports one or more accepted
   concepts.
9. Use `merged_into` when a candidate should not stand alone but is represented
   by one accepted concept.
10. Use `pruned` only when the candidate should not influence the lesson concept
   set at all. Use only a reason from `controlled_pruning_reasons`.
11. Do not prune a distinct teachable idea as a duplicate unless an accepted
   concept in this same response actually represents it. Never justify pruning
   by saying another cluster, later batch, or future step will handle the idea.
12. Avoid `review`. Phase 4 has no human review escape hatch. If the lesson
   metadata, candidate description, source roles, and coverage criteria are
   sufficient, decide accepted, merged, or pruned.
13. Use `review` only when the input is structurally impossible to interpret.
   Phase 4b will treat any review output as unresolved work requiring repair.

## Quality Repair Workflow

For `task: lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`:

1. Evaluate only `target_candidate_ids`; do not rewrite the whole Lesson.
2. Use `current_reconciled_candidates` to decide whether a target candidate is
   already represented.
3. Create `new_accepted_concepts` only for target candidates that represent
   lesson-worthy teachable ideas not already covered.
4. Use `existing_concept_candidate_additions` when a target candidate is
   represented by an existing reconciled concept.
5. Use `pruned` only when the target candidate should not influence the Lesson.
6. Never return `review`. A hard choice must still become accepted, merged, or
   pruned with a clear explanation.
7. Do not use a duplicate or near-duplicate reason unless the target candidate
   is represented by an existing or new accepted concept in this response.

## Clustering Output Contract

For `task: lesson_candidate_clustering`, return one valid JSON object only:

```json
{
  "clusters": [
    {
      "id": "cluster_001",
      "label": "Short cluster label",
      "rationale": "Why these candidates may describe the same teachable idea.",
      "candidate_ids": ["compact-candidate-id"]
    }
  ]
}
```

## Evaluation Output Contract

For `task: lesson_cluster_evaluation`, return one valid JSON object only. Cover
all candidates in the provided cluster batch:

```json
{
  "accepted_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "lr001",
      "label": "Specific lesson-local teachable idea",
      "description": "What the student needs to understand in this Lesson.",
      "coverage_criteria": ["Observable check in one to three focused questions."],
      "source_candidate_ids": ["compact-candidate-id"],
      "merge_rationale": "Why these candidates form one lesson-local concept."
    }
  ],
  "candidate_assignments": [
    {
      "candidate_id": "compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "used_in",
      "accepted_ids": ["lr001"]
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "represented-candidate-id",
      "status": "merged_into",
      "merged_into": "lr001",
      "explanation": "Why it is represented by lr001 instead of standing alone."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "discarded-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "incidental",
      "explanation": "Why this candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "discarded-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "unrelated",
      "explanation": "Why this candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    }
  ]
}
```

## Quality Repair Output Contract

For `task: lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`, return one valid JSON object
only:

```json
{
  "new_accepted_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "repair001",
      "label": "Specific lesson-local teachable idea",
      "description": "What the student needs to understand in this Lesson.",
      "coverage_criteria": ["Observable check in one to three focused questions."],
      "source_candidate_ids": ["target-compact-candidate-id"],
      "merge_rationale": "Why these target candidates form a lesson-local concept."
    }
  ],
  "existing_concept_candidate_additions": [
    {
      "reconciled_candidate_id": "existing-final-reconciled-candidate-id",
      "candidate_ids": ["target-compact-candidate-id"],
      "explanation": "Why the target candidate is already represented."
    }
  ],
  "candidate_assignments": [
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "used_in",
      "accepted_ids": ["repair001"],
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate is accepted."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "merged_into",
      "merged_into": "existing-final-reconciled-candidate-id",
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate is represented by an existing concept."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "low_teaching_value",
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    }
  ]
}
```

## Self-check

- For clustering, every `input_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once across
  all cluster `candidate_ids`.
- For evaluation, every `input_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once in
  `candidate_assignments`.
- Every `used_in` or `merged_into` assignment references accepted concept IDs
  that also list that candidate in `source_candidate_ids`.
- A candidate may support multiple accepted concepts with `used_in`.
- A `pruned` or `review` candidate must not appear in any accepted concept's
  `source_candidate_ids`.
- Every pruned near-duplicate must be represented by an accepted concept in this
  response, or it should not be pruned as a duplicate.
- For quality repair, every `target_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once in
  `candidate_assignments`, and no assignment has `status: review`.
- If several accepted concepts are mainly setup, environment, licensing,
  administration, career guidance, or generic programming basics, re-check the
  Lesson metadata before accepting them.
- Before returning, ask whether the accepted concept set would let the Companion
  tutor the Lesson described by the metadata without major off-topic detours or
  missing central teachable distinctions.
- Do not emit dependencies, lesson segments, final Concept IDs, bridge concepts,
  subject-level merge decisions, or runtime graph fields.

cluster.label: Building an MLP for regression
cluster.rationale: These candidates describe creating a regression neural network with Dense layers where the output layer omits activation to predict continuous values.

clusters.label: Building an MLP for regression
clusters.rationale: These candidates describe creating a regression neural network with Dense layers where the output layer omits activation to predict continuous values.

clusters.label: Building a CNN in Keras
clusters.rationale: These candidates outline constructing a convolutional neural network with Conv2D, Activation, MaxPooling2D, Dropout, Flatten, and Dense layers, a standard CNN architecture.

clusters.label: Building an RNN with LSTM
clusters.rationale: These candidates describe building a recurrent network with an Embedding layer, an LSTM layer with dropout, and a Dense output for binary classification on sequential data.

clusters.label: Loading external data from URL
clusters.rationale: These candidates show how to fetch a dataset from a URL using urllib and np.loadtxt, a technique for loading external CSV data into NumPy arrays for training.

clusters.label: Keras on Kaggle Kernels (no local setup)
clusters.rationale: These candidates explain using Kaggle Kernels as a cloud environment with Keras pre-installed, eliminating local installation steps and offering immediate practice.

clusters.label: TensorFlow definition and history
clusters.rationale: These candidates introduce TensorFlow: open-source ML platform by Google, its computational graph approach, origin from Google Brain, and its release timeline.

clusters.label: TensorFlow ecosystem and components
clusters.rationale: These candidates discuss the broader TensorFlow ecosystem, including TF.js, TF Lite, TFX, and other tools, emphasizing flexibility and deployment options.

clusters.label: TensorBoard visualization tool
clusters.rationale: These candidates describe TensorBoard as a suite of visualization tools for monitoring and debugging ML models, often used alongside TensorFlow.

clusters.label: TensorFlow Hub pre-trained models
clusters.rationale: These candidates explain TensorFlow Hub as a repository of reusable pre-trained models, simplifying transfer learning and model deployment.

clusters.label: Machine learning model definition
clusters.rationale: These candidates define what a machine learning model is (a file trained on data to recognize patterns) and its role in making predictions.

clusters.label: TensorFlow Playground
clusters.rationale: These candidates introduce TensorFlow Playground as an interactive web-based tool for experimenting with neural networks, useful for learning.

clusters.label: TensorFlow competitors (PyTorch, etc.)
clusters.rationale: These candidates list major alternatives to TensorFlow (e.g., PyTorch, CNTK, MXNet) and briefly compare their strengths, providing context in the ML landscape.

candidates.label: Building an MLP for regression
candidates.description: Use Dense layers without activation on the output to perform regression with a neural network.
coverage_criteria: Student can create a regression MLP by omitting activation on the final Dense layer.
Student can explain why no activation is needed for regression output.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The 'Regression' subsection demonstrates a two‑layer MLP where the output Dense layer has no activation function specified.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This tiny architectural variation can be assessed by asking to build a regression model.

candidates.label: Building a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) in Keras
candidates.description: Construct a CNN using Conv2D for convolution, Activation layers, MaxPooling2D for downsampling, Dropout for regularization, Flatten, and Dense layers.
coverage_criteria: Student can stack Conv2D, Activation('relu'), and MaxPooling2D layers.
Student can explain the role of Flatten before the Dense classifier.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The 'Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)' section provides a complete architecture with Conv2D, MaxPooling2D, Dropout, Flatten, and Dense.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This candidate covers the unique CNN layer patterns; several coding questions can target individual components.

candidates.label: Building a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) with LSTM
candidates.description: Create an RNN by adding an Embedding layer to handle integer sequences and an LSTM layer with dropout parameters, followed by a Dense output for binary classification.
coverage_criteria: Student can add Embedding and LSTM layers to a Sequential model.
Student can explain the purpose of dropout and recurrent_dropout in LSTM.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The 'Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)' subsection shows a model with Embedding, LSTM, and Dense with sigmoid activation.
rationale.granularity_rationale: The three‑layer RNN is a compact unit that can be tested by asking for its implementation and parameter explanation.

candidates.label: Loading external data from a URL with NumPy
candidates.description: Use urllib.request.urlopen and np.loadtxt to fetch a CSV dataset directly from a URL and split it into feature matrix X and target vector y.
coverage_criteria: Student can write the code to open a URL, load its content as a NumPy array, and slice the columns into features and labels.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The 'Other' subsection under 'Data' provides a concrete example of using urlopen and np.loadtxt on a specific diabetes dataset URL.
rationale.granularity_rationale: The task involves two specific functions; it is small enough to test with a prompt like 'load a dataset from this URL'.

candidates.label: Using Kaggle Kernels for Keras without local installation
candidates.description: Kaggle Kernels provide a cloud-based Python environment with Keras pre-installed, allowing users to start building models immediately without any setup.
coverage_criteria: Describe how Kaggle Kernels eliminate the need for local installation of Keras.
State that Keras is available by default in Kaggle Python environments.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly demonstrates using Kaggle Kernels, noting that you don't have to install or configure anything, and shows the Kernel UI.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a single, practical piece of knowledge about a tool that enables immediate hands-on practice, easily checkable with a short question.

candidates.label: What is TensorFlow?
candidates.description: TensorFlow is an open-source platform for machine learning, developed by Google, providing a flexible ecosystem with tools, libraries, and community resources for building and deploying ML applications.
coverage_criteria: State that TensorFlow is an open-source platform for machine learning.
Identify Google as its creator.
Explain that it offers a flexible ecosystem for building and deploying ML models.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly introduces TensorFlow as an open-source platform by Google for machine learning with a flexible ecosystem.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a foundational idea that can be assessed with a few direct questions to ensure understanding of TensorFlow's basic identity.

candidates.label: TensorFlow's computational graph approach
candidates.description: At its core, TensorFlow is an open-source library for numerical computation using computational graphs, which facilitates developing and training machine learning models.
coverage_criteria: Explain that TensorFlow uses computational graphs for numerical computation.
Describe that this approach helps in developing and training ML models.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video states that TensorFlow's core is a library for numerical computation using computational graphs, which aids ML model development.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This concept is specific enough to check understanding of TensorFlow's underlying mechanism without overwhelming detail.

candidates.label: History of TensorFlow
candidates.description: TensorFlow was developed by the Google Brain team with the mission to make machines intelligent. It became open-source in 2015 and version 1.0 was released in February 2017.
coverage_criteria: Name the team that created TensorFlow (Google Brain).
State the year TensorFlow became open-source (2015).
State the year of version 1.0 release (2017).

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video mentions the Google Brain team, open-sourcing in 2015, and v1.0 in 2017.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a small set of facts that can be quizzed effectively.

candidates.label: DistBelief
candidates.description: Before TensorFlow, Google used DistBelief for deep learning, but it had limitations in usability and flexibility, leading to TensorFlow's creation.
coverage_criteria: Identify DistBelief as Google's original deep learning tool.
Explain why TensorFlow was created (to overcome DistBelief's limitations).

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly mentions DistBelief as the predecessor and its flaws.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a specific historical point that can be checked with a couple of questions.

candidates.label: Flexibility of TensorFlow
candidates.description: TensorFlow is designed to be flexible, efficient, extensible, and portable, running on devices from smartphones to large clusters, and supporting deployment in cloud, local, browser, or device environments.
coverage_criteria: List the design goals of TensorFlow (flexible, efficient, extensible, portable).
Give examples of deployment targets (smartphone, cluster, cloud, browser, local).

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video emphasizes TensorFlow's flexibility and portability across various devices and environments.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This concept captures the platform's design philosophy, which is important for understanding its use cases.

candidates.label: Key components of TensorFlow ecosystem
candidates.description: The TensorFlow ecosystem includes TensorFlow Core, TensorFlow.js for JavaScript, TensorFlow Lite for mobile/IoT, TensorFlow Extended (TFX) for production pipelines, and Swift for TensorFlow.
coverage_criteria: Name at least three components of the TensorFlow ecosystem.
Describe the primary purpose of each named component.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video lists and explains these components in a dedicated section.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Knowing these components is essential for understanding the scope of TensorFlow's offerings and can be assessed with a few identification tasks.

candidates.label: TensorBoard
candidates.description: TensorBoard is a suite of visualization tools for machine learning that displays graphs, metrics, data, images, and audio to help understand and debug models.
coverage_criteria: Explain what TensorBoard is.
List at least two types of data it can visualize.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video describes TensorBoard as a tool for visualization of data and experiments.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a single tool with a clear purpose, suitable for a focused check.

candidates.label: TensorFlow Hub
candidates.description: TensorFlow Hub is a library of pre-trained machine learning models that can be easily reused in projects, such as text classification models.
coverage_criteria: Describe the purpose of TensorFlow Hub.
Explain how a pre-trained model can be imported using code (e.g., hub.Module).

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video explains TensorFlow Hub and shows a code snippet using hub.Module.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This concept focuses on a specific resource for model reuse, testable with a code-related question.

candidates.label: ML Model Definition
candidates.description: A machine learning model is a file trained on a dataset to recognize patterns, which can then be used to make predictions on new data.
coverage_criteria: Define a machine learning model.
Explain the role of a dataset in training.
Provide an example of a trained model's application (e.g., dog breed identification).

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video defines a model, explains training with datasets, and gives an illustrative example.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a core concept in ML that can be assessed with a definition and example.

candidates.label: TensorFlow Playground
candidates.description: TensorFlow Playground is an interactive web-based tool that allows users to experiment with neural networks directly in the browser.
coverage_criteria: Describe what TensorFlow Playground is.
Explain its purpose for learning about neural networks.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video mentions TensorFlow Playground as a browser-based neural network sandbox.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a specific hands-on tool that can be easily verified with a brief description.

candidates.label: Competitors to TensorFlow
candidates.description: Major alternatives to TensorFlow include PyTorch (Python, good for smaller projects), CNTK (Microsoft Cognitive Toolkit, focused on deep learning), Apache MXNet (AWS's main DL framework), and Caffe (open-source DL framework).
coverage_criteria: Name at least two competitors of TensorFlow.
Briefly describe one key characteristic of each.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video lists several competitors and their niches.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This concept provides a comparative perspective, testable by naming and describing alternatives.

accepted_concepts.label: Specific teachable idea
accepted_concepts.description: What the student needs to understand.
coverage_criteria: Observable check in one to three focused questions.
accepted_concepts.merge_rationale: Why these candidates belong together or stand alone.

candidate_assignments.explanation: Why it should not stand alone but is represented by the accepted concept.
Why this candidate should not influence the graph.
Why this candidate should not influence the graph.

output_contract.review_policy: Do not use review except for structurally impossible inputs; Phase 4b repairs review outputs.

web_access_policy.instruction: Do not use web search or open URLs. Use only the provided candidate cards.
